items.title: Neutrons, death metal and a tiny prehistoric dragon: Scans reveal new horned reptile species from 156 million years ago
items.desc: An unassuming fossil discovery in Wyoming caused quite a stir: Was it a baby dinosaur, a prehistoric snake or perhaps an entirely new species? Neutron imaging at the Paul Scherrer Institute PSI and the trained eye of a paleontologist eventually provided the answer: the 156-million-year-old fossil is that of a previously unknown species of reptile.

items.title: Diplomacy, humor and avoidance—what we found when we investigated friendships across class divides
items.desc: Several years ago, the U.S. economist Raj Chetty and his team at Harvard University analyzed billions of ties on Facebook in a bid to learn more about social mobility. Their findings highlighted an important link between cross-class friendship and social mobility. Specifically, they found that people from low-income backgrounds who have more friends from wealthier backgrounds tend to have better chances of earning more as adults.

items.title: Newly discovered gut viruses offer clues to the origins of the smallpox virus family
items.desc: Human and animal digestive systems host vast communities of microorganisms, including bacteria and viruses. Some are harmful, others are beneficial, and many remain poorly understood. In a recent study, scientists found an entirely new group of viruses without even having to go anywhere near anyone's innards.

items.title: Artificial wetland near Valencia traps 36% of incoming microplastics, study finds
items.desc: The Tancat de la Pipa, an artificial wetland designed as a "green filter" for the Albufera de València, reduces microplastic pollution in the natural lagoon by 36%, according to research conducted by the Institute of Water and Environmental Engineering (IIAMA) at the Universitat Politècnica de València (UPV) and the Faculty of Environmental Sciences and Engineering at Babe–Bolyai University in Romania published in the journal Applied Sciences.

items.title: Black gobies are growing larger despite climate change
items.desc: Researchers at the Department of Paleontology at the University of Vienna compared fossil and modern ear stones of the black goby (Gobius niger) from the northern Adriatic Sea to reconstruct its growth history over the past 8,000 years. The surprising result: while body size remained remarkably stable in the past, today's black gobies grow faster and reach larger sizes—even as the Adriatic Sea is warming rapidly. The study is now published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

items.title: New metal-organic material combines metallic conductivity with promise for light-sensing electronics
items.desc: In modern electronics and computing, finding advanced materials that can efficiently move electrical charges without losing energy remains a critical scientific challenge. While traditional metals conduct electricity exceptionally well, researchers continually seek innovative hybrid materials that combine the design flexibility of chemistry with true metallic performance.

items.title: Duck-billed dinosaur discovered in Italy had a birdlike beak hidden among its bizarre 'spikes'
items.desc: For more than 15 years, the Italian duck-billed dinosaur Tethyshadros insularis has been reconstructed with one of the most unusual mouth structures among hadrosauroids. The tip of its upper jaw featured three forward-pointing bony projections on each side, long interpreted as exposed "spikes" or toothlike beak ornaments. However, a new study published in Royal Society Open Science reveals that this interpretation was incorrect.

items.title: Confirmed: Numbers tell, but language sells
items.desc: Suppose you are in charge of your firm's commuting policy and, after some research, you determine that 57% of your colleagues drive to work. How would you communicate that number to coworkers?

items.title: Decoding interactomes: Supercomputing predicts bacterial protein links from shared evolutionary patterns
items.desc: Predicting how proteins interact inside a cell is essential to understanding how organisms function and why they differ from one another, yet experimental hurdles and the computational cost of analyzing millions of protein pairs make it impossible to explore complete interaction networks, particularly in understudied bacteria and organisms.

items.title: Mandatory minimum sentencing oftentimes means 10 more months in prison, study finds
items.desc: Racial minorities facing federal drug charges have allegations of conspiracy added to their cases at higher rates than their white counterparts, as prosecutors seek to push them over the threshold for a mandatory minimum sentence that then can be used in negotiating stiffer penalties, a new UConn study finds.

items.title: Lunar sample research yields new discoveries, revealing the history of the moon's largest impact basin
items.desc: An international research team led by geologists from the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences (DEPS) at The University of Hong Kong (HKU) has uncovered new evidence of how the moon's largest impact basin, the South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin, formed and evolved over billions of years.

items.title: Museum specimens yield new subspecies of New Zealand bush wren decades after its extinction
items.desc: Ecosystems can buffer the impacts of climate change and humans for only so long before an ecological turning point is reached, a new study on Aotearoa New Zealand's extinct mātuhituhi—bush wren—has highlighted.

items.title: Why stopover sites are vital for migratory birds as spring arrives earlier
items.desc: Stopover sites are more than just places for migratory birds to rest and refuel. They also help birds adapt to climate change, according to research by Leiden ecologist Yali Si.

items.title: From broken circuits to growing graphite: A new role for electromigration
items.desc: Inside electronic devices, electric current can gradually displace atoms within tiny metal connections, creating gaps or unwanted accumulations that eventually cause circuits to fail. This phenomenon, known as electromigration, has long been regarded as a reliability problem that engineers must work to prevent. Yet the ability of an electric current to move atoms also raises the possibility of putting that movement to constructive use, directing atoms through a material rather than allowing them to migrate uncontrollably.

items.title: Microplastics make up 1 in 100 airborne particles sampled at four Michigan schools
items.desc: One in 100 of the tiny particles hanging in the air we breathe in Michigan is a microplastic, according to a University of Michigan study. The study tested the air for microplastics in four locations across lower Michigan, all in the parking lots of K-12 schools. It found that microplastics constitute about 1% of particles found in the atmosphere.

items.title: Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins
items.desc: A new study has uncovered a surprising concern hiding in popular plant-based foods and drinks. Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk, and soy milk, and found that every single one contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin. Known as mycotoxins, these naturally occurring compounds can contaminate grains, legumes, and seeds during farming and storage.

items.title: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history
items.desc: A bizarre whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so dramatically crooked that scientists believe it may have been the most asymmetrical of any mammal. Discovered in Peru, the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had an enormous downward-curving snout and a skull so distorted that researchers initially thought it had been damaged after death. Instead, its strange anatomy appears to have been an extraordinary evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.

items.title: Is free will an illusion? New brain research reveals a surprising twist
items.desc: New research reveals that the brain makes free choices and forced decisions using surprisingly similar neural processes, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The discovery challenges assumptions about free will while suggesting that our personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.

items.title: Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut
items.desc: The secret behind truly terrible-smelling farts lies in tiny amounts of sulfur-containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists reveal why some foods make farts smell worse, why loud farts aren't always the stinkiest, and how our noses evolved to detect these powerful odors.

items.title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
items.desc: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

items.title: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible
items.desc: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible depending on something unexpected: tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say this discovery could help make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.

items.title: This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
items.desc: More than 300 million years ago, long before dinosaurs roamed Earth, the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape teeming with bizarre creatures. Now, scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor, revealing new clues about the evolution of frogs and salamanders.

items.title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
items.desc: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.

items.title: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K
items.desc: Deep-sea researchers have captured stunning new footage of an extraordinarily rare fish with a transparent head and rotating eyes nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface. Known as the barreleye fish, this bizarre creature uses its upward-pointing eyes to spot prey before rotating them forward to track its next meal, all while a transparent dome protects them.

items.title: Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search
items.desc: A major new investigation into Stonehenge’s mysterious six-ton Altar Stone has uncovered fresh clues while ruling out several suspected sources. Once thought to have originated in Wales, the massive sandstone slab is now believed to have come from northeastern Scotland, although researchers have yet to find an exact match.

items.title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why
items.desc: Scientists may have finally explained why up to more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from rocks around the world. New research suggests that powerful currents deep inside the planet slowly raised and lowered entire continents, allowing erosion to erase vast stretches of geological history before they were buried and preserved.

items.title: New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors
items.desc: A major breakthrough in superconductivity research has revealed that one of the essential ingredients for electricity to flow without resistance can exist at room temperature. Scientists discovered that electrons can form stable pairs at much higher temperatures than previously understood, suggesting that a different obstacle may be preventing room-temperature superconductivity.

items.title: NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world
items.desc: A European spacecraft has revealed a mysterious, crater-covered side of the asteroid Didymos as it prepares to investigate the aftermath of NASA’s historic 2022 asteroid impact. The mission could uncover new clues about the collision and help turn asteroid deflection into a powerful defense against future threats to Earth.

items.title: A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics
items.desc: Scientists have spotted hints of a mysterious rotation in the universe’s oldest light that could reveal new physics and shed light on dark matter and dark energy. A new technique developed at UC San Diego could help rule out misleading telescope errors, bringing researchers closer to determining whether the strange signal is real.

items.title: The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected
items.desc: Scientists have discovered that psychopathic traits are associated with surprisingly different patterns of language, with some individuals using more positive words and others expressing greater negativity or less anxiety. The findings challenge familiar stereotypes about psychopathy and suggest that the stories people tell about their lives may offer important clues about their personalities.

items.title: China Ratchets Up Its Weaponization of Trade
items.desc: Just as the US has been leveraging its large market and technological leadership for geopolitical ends, China is now using its dominance in critical minerals, industrial inputs, and specialized manufacturing machinery to coerce and punish other countries. The consequences, both economic and geopolitical, are far-reaching.

items.title: There Is Only One Thing to Talk About With Russia
items.desc: The European security order’s foundational principle is never to tolerate aggression. There is no need to revise that order, as the Kremlin has proposed, only to wait for a Russian regime that is willing to respect other countries’ territorial integrity and uphold its own previous commitments.

items.title: The Truth About Global AI Governance
items.desc: Because the current approach to global AI governance presumes that developing countries are full of eager adopters of AI who need to be cautioned about the technology's risks, it overlooks what their information environments and media markets actually need. A survey of researchers who study 71 countries sets the record straight.

items.title: Demography is the Achilles’ Heel of Dictatorships
items.desc: Governments that manipulate population figures often end up deceiving themselves as much as the public. When autocratic leaders mistake inflated numbers for real national strength, they make costly strategic mistakes and fail to address their countries’ demographic decline until it is too late.

items.title: The Silver Lining of a Data-Center Slowdown
items.desc: With leading AI labs under intense competitive pressure to keep advancing the frontier of the technology's capabilities, resistance to the build-out of computing resources is not such a bad thing. The more time we can buy, the greater our chances of maximizing the potential benefits and mitigating the risks.

items.title: What Nvidia’s Crisis Reveals About the Chip War
items.desc: Export restrictions, like those depriving China of Nvidia’s most advanced chips, may buy time by curtailing a competitor's access to frontier capabilities made elsewhere. But in any technological conflict, policymakers must remember that slowing a rival is not the same as strengthening oneself.

items.title: When Export Restraints Are the Lesser Evil
items.desc: Governments face pressure to protect domestic industries while preserving access to cheaper foreign goods. The recent EU-China car-export deal offers an uneasy compromise that protects European automakers while keeping Chinese cars available to consumers, making it preferable to prohibitive tariffs.

items.title: The Trade Losses That Nobody Counts
items.desc: While much of the United Kingdom’s post-Brexit debate has focused on the monetary value of lost trade with the European Union, the composition of UK-EU trade flows warrants closer attention. A sharp decline in the variety of products shipped to Europe suggests that the economic costs have been greater than many realize.

items.title: Nigeria’s Big Bet on Health Care
items.desc: Nigeria’s dependence on imported medicines and medical equipment leaves families exposed to exchange-rate fluctuations and hospitals at the mercy of global supply chains. Expanding domestic manufacturing is essential to reducing the cost of treatment and ensuring that more Nigerians can access quality care.

items.title: What Should the Nvidia Board Do?
items.desc: The proper role of any corporate board is to strike a careful balance between stakeholders. In Nvidia's case, the board will have to consider not just the current trading price, but also how its decisions will affect the landscape in which it operates, its employees, and its license to trade.

items.title: The Roots of Macron’s Failure
items.desc: Although French President Emmanuel Macron has certainly made mistakes, his troubled presidency is symptomatic of a deeper problem. In the end, he failed to build something truly enduring because he was seduced by the same monarchical impulse that is a recurring feature of French political culture.

items.title: Yalta in Shenzhen?
items.desc: In principle, the planned summit of the US, Russian, and Chinese presidents could usefully address what should be done to limit the proliferation of nuclear weapons, ensure that AI is more a force for good than harm, and end ongoing wars and prevent new ones. But principle is one thing; in practice, we are likely to see something else.

items.title: The Perverse Effects of the AI Investment Boom
items.desc: As big tech companies increasingly turn to debt markets to finance massive investments in AI data centers, they are competing for the same pools of capital as many governments. With interest rates already high and public demands for spending on the rise, the timing could hardly be worse for vulnerable economies.

items.title: Oceania’s Three Goals for COP31
items.desc: To make COP31 the “Blue COP,” delegates must recommit to keeping the 1.5° Celsius warming goal alive, reform the climate-finance system, and address our dependence on the fossil fuels driving the ocean's warming and acidification. Pacific countries have long championed these causes, but now the rest of the world must join them.

items.title: How to navigate the world with two halves of one brain
items.desc: Psychiatrist Iain McGilchrist has spent 35 years studying how the brain shapes consciousness. In this full interview, he explains why the two hemispheres attend to the world in radically different ways, and how one narrow, grasping mode has come to dominate Western civilization. He then explores the nature of reality: a creative cosmos that flows at the edge of chaos, where consciousness is primary and matter is one of its phases.
